root_cause.text: The `sev_es_sync_vmsa()` function lacked validation to prevent synchronizing vCPU state to an already-encrypted VMSA, allowing kernel code to write to guest-private memory protected by the RMP (Reverse Map Protection) on SNP-enabled systems, which triggers an RMP violation and host panic.
root_cause.evidence: The patch adds a check `if (vcpu->arch.guest_state_protected) return -EINVAL;` at the beginning of `sev_es_sync_vmsa()` to reject the operation when the VMSA has already been encrypted (indicated by `guest_state_protected` flag). The CVE description explicitly states that on SNP-enabled hosts, accessing guest-private memory generates an RMP #PF that panics the host, and the stack trace shows the panic occurs in `sev_es_sync_vmsa()` called from `snp_launch_update_vmsa()`. Without this guard, the function proceeds to write to encrypted guest memory, violating RMP protections.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add early validation to reject VMSA synchronization attempts when guest state is already protected.
intent_record.what: Added a guard clause at the beginning of sev_es_sync_vmsa() that checks if vcpu->arch.guest_state_protected is true and returns -EINVAL if so, before any other validation logic executes.
intent_record.how: This change prevents the VMSA synchronization function from proceeding when the guest state is already marked as protected. It short-circuits execution early, avoiding unnecessary processing and potential state corruption by rejecting the operation with an error code when called in an invalid state.

grouping_result.intent: Add early validation to reject VMSA synchronization attempts when guest state is already protected.

relevance_review.reason: The group directly addresses the vulnerability root cause by adding early validation to prevent synchronization of vCPU state to an already-encrypted VMSA. This prevents kernel code from attempting to write to guest-private memory protected by RMP, which was the core issue causing RMP violations and host panics on SNP-enabled systems.

bic_trace_step.reason: The function `sev_es_sync_vmsa()` writes to the VMSA (Virtual Machine Save Area) pointed to by `svm->sev_es.vmsa` without validating whether the VMSA has already been encrypted. The vulnerability root cause states that the function lacks validation to prevent synchronizing vCPU state to an already-encrypted VMSA. In this commit, there is no check to verify the encryption state of the VMSA before performing the memcpy at line 574 and subsequent register synchronization operations (lines 577-601). On SNP-enabled systems with RMP protection, writing to an already-encrypted VMSA (guest-private memory) triggers an RMP violation and host panic. The only validation present is for debug-related fields (lines 565-566), which does not address the core vulnerability of writing to an already-encrypted save area.

bic_trace_step.reason: The `sev_es_sync_vmsa()` function (lines 513-555) lacks validation to check if the VMSA has already been encrypted before attempting to sync vCPU state to it. The function performs checks on debug fields (line 519: `if (svm->vcpu.guest_debug || (save->dr7 & ~DR7_FIXED_1))`) but has no check to prevent re-synchronization to an already-encrypted VMSA. The vulnerability root cause states that the function should validate to prevent synchronizing to an already-encrypted VMSA, which would trigger RMP violations on SNP systems. The code directly writes to `svm->vmsa` via `memcpy(svm->vmsa, save, sizeof(*save))` at line 551 without any guard condition checking if the VMSA is already protected/encrypted. This is the vulnerable construct - the absence of a check like `if (svm->vcpu.arch.guest_state_protected)` before performing the sync operation.
